title: We Shall Outlast Them: Putin’s Global Campaign to Defeat the West
gist: A review of Hanna Notte's book on Russia's post-2022 strategy of outlasting Western sanctions by reorienting toward India, Africa, and the post-Soviet space, while noting the strategy's real limits (BRICS, Syria) and its long-term developmental cost to Russia.

insights.claim: Russia has shown resilience against Western sanctions imposed since its 2022 full-scale invasion of Ukraine, avoiding the economic collapse some Western strategists hoped to induce.
insights.speaker: Foreign Affairs
insights.so_what: Sanctions-based strategies against large, resource-rich autocracies may take far longer to bite than policymakers assume; investors should not price in near-term Russian economic collapse.
insights.quote: Notte, an international relations scholar, describes Russia’s resilience in the face of Western efforts to starve its economy through sanctions

insights.claim: Moscow's post-2022 foreign policy is a deliberate bid to reorient away from the West toward the east and south, reasserting itself as a major global power rather than accepting isolation.
insights.speaker: Foreign Affairs
insights.so_what: Frames Russia's geopolitical posture as an active pivot strategy, not merely defensive retrenchment; relevant to positioning on Russia-adjacent trade and diplomatic flows.

insights.claim: Russia is capitalizing on the Soviet Union's anticolonial legacy to build stronger ties with India and various African countries.
insights.speaker: Foreign Affairs
insights.so_what: Historical anticolonial branding gives Russia a durable soft-power advantage over Western competitors in parts of the Global South, complicating Western efforts to isolate Moscow diplomatically.
insights.quote: Traveling far and wide, Notte provides a firsthand account of Russia’s efforts to strengthen ties with India and various African countries, where it capitalizes on the Soviet legacy of anticolonialism.

insights.claim: Maintaining influence over post-Soviet states remains a core, near-abroad priority for the Kremlin even as it courts more distant partners.
insights.speaker: Foreign Affairs
insights.so_what: Signals continued Russian pressure on Central Asia, the Caucasus, and other former Soviet states as a persistent geopolitical risk factor.

insights.claim: Despite courting BRICS members, Moscow failed to turn the bloc (originally Brazil, Russia, India, China, and South Africa) into a cohesive anti-Western diplomatic force.
insights.speaker: Foreign Affairs
insights.so_what: Undercuts the narrative of a unified BRICS-led counterweight to Western institutions; BRICS cohesion should not be overestimated as a geopolitical or trade-bloc risk.
insights.quote: Moscow failed to build a formidable diplomatic force out of BRICS—whose first five members were Brazil, Russia, India, China, and South Africa

insights.claim: Russia was unable to prevent the December 2024 overthrow of Syrian President Bashar al-Assad, a longtime ally and client, exposing real limits on Moscow's power-projection capacity.
insights.speaker: Foreign Affairs
insights.so_what: Loss of a decades-long Middle Eastern client despite military commitment signals genuine capacity constraints on Russian power abroad, not just Western propaganda framing.
insights.quote: or to prevent the 2024 overthrow of Syrian President Bashar al-Assad, a longtime ally

insights.claim: Even if Putin's resolve to outlast the West is unwavering, Russia's isolation from the West is imposing a high cost on the country's long-term economic development.
insights.speaker: Foreign Affairs
insights.so_what: Investors weighing long-horizon Russia exposure should discount near-term geopolitical resilience against a structurally weakening growth and technology base.
insights.quote: Putin’s resolve to outlast the West may be unwavering, but Russia’s isolation from the West comes at a high cost to the country’s long-term development.
